items.title: Oil prices ease 3% on optimism for Qatari-led talks on ending Iran war

events.article_text:
Oil Prices Slide 3% as Hopes for Iran Peace Deal Grow

What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

Crude oil prices started the week with a dip on renewed optimism about a possible peace deal between the United States and Iran, following reports about mediation talks between Iran and Qatar over the weekend.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $109.82 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was changing hands for $100.57 per barrel, despite a statement by Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi that said Tehran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy", as cited by Reuters.

ING commodity strategists, meanwhile, noted separate reports about President Trump signaling he was ready to “give diplomacy a chance” but added that “The price action in oil in recent weeks reflects a market increasingly bracing for the potential for more hostilities between the US and Iran.” Besides, Trump has also indicated in recent days that he was ready to resume hostilities.

“Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now,” KCM Trade’s chief market analyst Tim Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters earlier today. Whether these hopes are justified should become clear soon enough, and that will set the tone for oil prices for the rest of the year.

In case of an escalation, the price direction is clear enough. In the absence of new U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, some of the upward potential would be gone. The question is how much and for how long, assuming the Iranian-Qatari talks fail to result in a path to a firm peace agreement. With Iran insisting that all its conditions for a peace deal must be met and the U.S. repeatedly indicating it is disinclined to do that, chances are a failure is the most likely outcome of those talks.

analysis.tldr: Global crude oil prices are falling because people hope peace talks between the U.S. and Iran might ease Middle East tensions, which generally helps lower fuel import costs for India.
the_story: Crude oil prices slid by 3% at the start of the week, with Brent crude trading at $109.82 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $100.57 per barrel.
The price drop was driven by renewed optimism from mediation talks between Iran and Qatar over the weekend.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi stated that Tehran was prepared for 'both defence and diplomacy'.

ING commodity strategists noted that President Trump signaled he was ready to 'give diplomacy a chance', though markets remain braced for potential hostilities since Trump also indicated he could resume hostilities.
Analysts caution that Iran insists all its conditions must be met while the U.S. is disinclined to do so, meaning the talks could easily fail.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices fell about 3% because traders are hopeful that peace talks involving Qatar, the U.S., and Iran might prevent a wider war. Prices had previously shot up because markets feared military conflict in the Middle East would disrupt oil supplies, but a quiet weekend without military escalation cooled those fears down.
analysis.analogy: It is like a neighborhood panic when people think a loud argument might turn into a street fight, causing everyone to hoard supplies. When a respected neighbor steps in to talk things out and the weekend stays quiet, people calm down and grocery prices stop spiking.
why_it_matters_india: Global oil prices drop due to easing conflict fears in the Middle East.
India imports a large share of its crude oil from overseas.
Cheaper oil lowers the total dollar bill India pays to buy fuel from abroad.
A lower import bill reduces pressure on the rupee (vs the US dollar) and helps keep inflation (general rise in prices) in check for everyday consumers.

impacts.rationale: Peace hopes and lack of weekend military escalation have taken the immediate heat out of oil markets, which is generally good for importing countries.
When oil prices fall, India needs fewer dollars to buy energy, which helps strengthen the rupee — making imported goods slightly cheaper.
Cheaper global oil eventually translates to lower transport and manufacturing costs at home, easing price pressures for ordinary people.

watch_next: Whether the diplomatic talks between Iran and Qatar actually produce a firm agreement or collapse
Future statements from U.S. and Iranian leaders regarding military actions or naval blockades
analysis.caveats: If the peace talks fail — which analysts note is a strong possibility given opposing demands — oil prices could quickly reverse course and spike again.

analysis.analogy: It is like a popular collectible item that everyone rushed to buy at very high prices earlier in the year, but as the cost of everyday things went up and other options started paying better rewards, people lost interest and its resale price dropped sharply.

Local retail gold investors see the value of their holdings shrink compared to January peaks.
Cautious market sentiment spreads as investors rethink their short-term expectations for precious metals.

events.headline: Conflict in the Red Sea is forcing cloud giants to find a new route for the internet

items.title: Conflict in the Red Sea is forcing cloud giants to find a new route for the internet
items.summary: Fishermen motor past a commercial vessel anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandeb, in the straits connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean on September 12, 2026. Yemen's Houthis took over on September 11, 2026, a Red Sea island of Mayyun that is located in the middle of the Bab al-Mandeb shipping lane, completing their push to control the area, a local government official and eyewitnesses told AFP. Hundreds of people have died since the Iran-backed Houthis launched an offensive around Bab al-Mandab, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports. (Photo by AFP via Getty Image

events.article_text:
U.S. cloud giants are facing steep prices to secure backup internet routes around the Red Sea as fighting rages over the Red Sea strait that carries most data cables between Europe and Asia.

More than 90% of data capacity between Europe and Asia runs through cables under the Red Sea. The cables enter the sea at Bab al-Mandab, a strait less than 32 kilometers (20 miles) wide between Yemen and the African nations of Djibouti and Eritrea.

The Houthis, a U.S.-designated terrorist organization, seized Yemen’s side of the strait in September, including the island of Mayyun. On October 5, Saudi-backed government forces said they had retaken key positions around the strait and the port of Mocha — claims the Houthis denied.

In September, Google bought a pair of fiber strands running along Turkish state pipelines, paying two to three times the roughly 6 million euros ($7 million) that newer lines crossing Turkey are expected to cost, said a person familiar with the deal, requesting anonymity because the details are not public. Long-distance fiber is usually sold with a single upfront payment covering 15 years or more of use. Buyers also pay a separate annual fee for maintenance.

Microsoft said on September 23 that it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and land links across the Middle East by 2030. Iraq also signed a contract with Qatari telecom company Ooredoo on September 10 to carry data toward Europe through an underground route from the southern port of Al-Faw.

Almost all major cloud companies are looking for backup routes around the Red Sea, the person told Rest of World. Google and Meta have started sending some live traffic through a land route across Iraq that they had previously held in reserve, the person said.

Google and Meta did not respond to Rest of World’s requests for comment by the time of publication.

With Yemen’s side of the strait now contested, a single cable cut there could take months to fix, because repair crews need permission and safety guarantees to work in the water, industry experts told Rest of World. Switching to another sea cable does not help because almost all of them pass through the same narrow gap, they said.

“You can have capacity on multiple cables, but if they’re all routed through the same tight expanse of water, suddenly your route resilience isn’t looking so resilient,” said Paul Brodsky, senior research manager at TeleGeography, a U.S. research firm that tracks telecommunications infrastructure worldwide. “The repair ship issue is very real.”

Three Red Sea cables were damaged in 2024, most likely by the anchor of a drifting cargo ship that a missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis had disabled. Those repairs took months because crews had to wait a long time for permits, Brodsky said.

“Depending on the availability of a repair ship, a cable repair might take one to two weeks,” Doug Madory, head of internet analysis at Santa Clara-based Infoblox, which runs core network services and tracks how internet traffic moves, told Rest of World. “But the last time there were cable cuts in this body of water, repairs took months because the repair ships needed assurances they would not be fired upon.”

Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon use about three-quarters of the world’s international internet bandwidth, according to TeleGeography. When Iranian drones struck Amazon’s data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in March, bank and payment apps in the region stopped working, and U.S. software company Snowflake reported service disruptions.

Since the start of September, cloud companies have been telling operators the minimum number of fiber strands they will start using, and by when, Martin Frank, a strategic adviser at IQ Networks, an Iraqi company that sells capacity on a fiber line it built from southern Iraq to the Turkish border, told Rest of World.

Cloud companies will likely test their land backups so they are ready if a sea cable breaks, Madory said. Until then, most of their data will keep flowing under the sea.

“Submarine cable routes are much cheaper, which is why they are so preferred,” he said. “I would expect land route alternatives to remain dormant until pressed into service due to a cable cut.”

Cloud companies have been hoping Yemen would settle down under a normal administration, Frank said. What would end that hope is what he called an Afghanistan scenario, in which the international community accepts the reality on the ground as the new normal.

“From what I see and hear, I would say that this scenario is getting more and more priced in by the day,” Frank said.

It may be some time before AI agents can fully navigate the complexities and cultural nuances of developing nations.

Chinese open-weight AI models offer high capability at significantly lower costs than U.S. frontier systems, but face monetization and compute challenges, experts said at a Rest of World event in San Francisco.

In his new book “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” writer Paris Marx examines how local communities are resisting the growing demand for water to cool data centers.

analysis.tldr: Internet costs for tech companies could rise as they pay extra for backup land routes around Red Sea fighting, potentially making digital services costlier for everyone.
the_story: More than 90% of data capacity between Europe and Asia runs through cables under the Red Sea, passing through the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait between Yemen, Djibouti, and Eritrea.
Fighting in Yemen has put the strait at risk, leading to three damaged Red Sea cables in 2024 and making it difficult for repair ships to safely enter the water.

U.S. cloud giants like Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are paying steep prices for backup land routes, with Google buying fiber strands along Turkish pipelines for two to three times the normal cost.
analysis.what_happened: Fighting over the Red Sea strait in Yemen has put vital underwater internet cables at risk. Because repairing damaged underwater cables now takes months due to safety risks from the conflict, big technology companies are rushing to secure expensive land-based backup internet routes.
analysis.analogy: It is like living on an island that only has one bridge to the mainland; when that bridge becomes unsafe, you have to pay a very high price to build a brand new ferry route just to stay connected.
why_it_matters_india: Tech giants face higher operating costs to secure alternative internet routes around the Red Sea.
These rising infrastructure and data-transport expenses are passed down to digital service providers and businesses.
Higher digital infrastructure costs can translate to costlier cloud services and tech subscriptions for Indian businesses and consumers.
This adds pressure to overall business operating costs across sectors that rely heavily on global cloud platforms.

impacts.rationale: higher operational costs for global cloud infrastructure could squeeze profit margins for tech service providers — bad for investors
costlier digital services and tech infrastructure filter into everyday consumer prices — bad for household budgets

watch_next: Further updates on Red Sea cable repairs and security in the Bab al-Mandab strait
Announcements from major tech companies regarding increased cloud service pricing
analysis.caveats: The article focuses primarily on U.S. tech giants and global internet cables, so the direct financial impact on Indian domestic companies remains indirect and limited for now.

events.headline: Singapore once thrived on chokepoints—now they could strangle the free port

items.title: Singapore once thrived on chokepoints—now they could strangle the free port
items.summary: The city-state's wealth rests on a vulnerability—its much larger neighbours' control over vital chokepoints. With Indonesia cutting pipeline gas supply amid a change in the tone of international relations towards seeking leverage by exploiting dependencies, Singapore may be facing stormy seas ahead

events.article_text:
Stand on a clear day atop Singapore’s Marina Bay Sands hotel and you can see the city-state’s promise and peril in a single glance.

In the foreground, a flotilla of ships lies at anchor, a reminder of how Singapore grew rich servicing immense global trade squeezed through the chokepoint of its narrow strait.

On the horizon, you can just make out the coastline of Indonesia, a country with almost 50 times Singapore’s population and 2,500 times as much land.

Its proximity is a reminder of how dependent that prosperity remains on good relations with Singapore’s much larger neighbours.

Such issues are top of mind right now. For weeks, the view has been obscured by a haze drifting across the water from wildfires on Indonesian islands. Singapore passed laws a decade ago to combat this recurring public-health catastrophe, but has struggled to enforce them amid intransigence from its neighbour.

Just days after the city announced measures against 10 Indonesian companies over the blazes this month, Jakarta started cutting pipeline supplies of natural gas to Singapore.

The decision may have an innocent explanation. Singapore has shifted towards LNG and away from Malaysian and Indonesian piped energy in recent years, anticipating that its neighbours will use more of their own supplies as their economies expand. A key link allowing Indonesia to divert gas locally was completed just weeks ago, and the affected exports represent less than 2% of daily demand.

But recent comments from Jakarta’s energy distribution minister don’t inspire confidence. He warned neighbouring countries to “be careful” about annoying Indonesia if they don’t want their exports cut off.

The whole episode is another unpleasant reminder of the vulnerability underlying Singapore’s prosperity. For more than two centuries, it has thrived as a free port, in a world where chokepoints to trade have been progressively dismantled.

The city was established by the British to bypass the Dutch stronghold in Java, and its most important nation-building projects in the 1960s and 1970s repeated the model by making it a key node of emerging commercial networks, from oil refining, to container shipping, to long-haul aviation.

Throughout all that, however, Singapore has remained acutely aware of the chokeholds its larger neighbours control. Political separation from Malaysia in 1965 raised fears of water supplies being cut off. A costly programme of desalination, recycling, harvesting and reservoir-building would now allow near-self-sufficiency in a crisis.

The same can’t be said for energy. Even LNG supplies could be severed by a naval blockade. Nuclear power has been considered, but comes with its own challenges: You could fit almost the entire nation inside the 20km mandatory-evacuation zone. Plans underway to install 4GW of solar panels by 2035 could leave about 5% of the country under silicon and glass, and still meet barely a 10th of electricity demand.

Separate plans to develop renewable projects and transmission lines stretching to Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, Indonesia and even Australia would at least diversify electricity suppliers. But those connections could, in theory, be cut off with the flick of a switch. Singapore’s driving role in establishing the power grid now taking shape across Asean can best be seen as an attempt to spread the risk across a web of mutual dependencies.

That’s the hopeful vision. In a world of multilateralism, peace and trade, small maritime republics can grow fabulously wealthy as nodes for global commerce and capital. Venice, an inspiration to Singapore’s founding generation, followed that model for centuries.

The worrying part is what came afterwards. As Europe’s commercial order gave way to an age of revolution, mass armies and nationalism, Venice’s wealth proved little protection against the larger powers surrounding it.

Napoleon extinguished the thousand-year republic in 1797 and it was traded back and forth like a bargaining chip between France and Austria for decades before being subsumed into the modern Italian state in 1866.

We could be entering a similar moment. The rising force in international relations is the chokepoint maximizer, looking for leverage over computer chips, critical minerals and trade flows to subdue its rivals. This year’s conflict over the Strait of Hormuz is a prime example. With barriers rising to commerce, migration and capital, free ports like Singapore are in lonely waters.

“If there were no international law and order, and big fish eat small fish and small fish eat shrimps, we wouldn’t exist,” founding father Lee Kuan Yew mused in 2007.

Lee’s successors must hope the great-power conflict brewing today is a passing storm, rather than a permanent shift in the global climate. ©Bloomberg

The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy.

analysis.tldr: Tensions over trade chokepoints and energy supplies in Southeast Asia remind investors that global trade disruptions can quickly ripple into higher energy import costs for countries like India.
the_story: Singapore grew rich as a free port servicing global trade, but remains deeply dependent on its much larger neighbor, Indonesia.
Recently, Indonesia cut pipeline supplies of natural gas to Singapore just days after Singapore announced measures against 10 Indonesian companies over smoke from wildfires.

Singapore's affected gas exports represent less than 2% of daily demand, and Singapore has been shifting toward LNG (liquefied natural gas, gas turned into liquid for easy shipping), but Indonesian officials warned neighbors to be careful about annoying them.

Historically, Singapore protected itself against water cutoffs through self-sufficiency, but energy remains a major vulnerability with limited alternatives like solar power and imported renewable energy cables.
The article warns that the world is moving away from free trade toward an era where big countries use trade chokepoints and leverage to control smaller neighbors.
analysis.what_happened: Singapore is facing geopolitical pressure as Indonesia cuts off some natural gas pipeline supplies following a dispute over wildfire smoke and environmental penalties. This highlights a fragile global environment where larger nations use trade chokeholds to exert power over smaller trading hubs, threatening the open global trade model that Singapore relies on.
analysis.analogy: It is like a small, successful corner shop that relies entirely on a grumpy mega-wholesaler next door for its electricity; if the wholesaler gets upset, they can flip the switch at any moment.
why_it_matters_india: Global trade routes and energy supplies face rising tensions as big nations weaponize trade chokeholds.
Energy shocks or restrictions in Asia can drive up global prices for natural gas and oil.
Higher global energy import costs push up domestic inflation (the rate at which prices rise) in energy-dependent developing nations like India.
Persistent global supply uncertainties can cause foreign investors to pull money out of emerging markets, affecting the rupee (the Indian currency).

impacts.target: Crude oil & energy import costs for India
impacts.rationale: As regional trade tensions rise and energy supplies face political restrictions, global energy prices can spike, making fuel imports costlier for India — bad for household budgets and inflation.
Global trade friction and energy shocks tend to strengthen the US dollar while pressuring emerging market currencies like the rupee, making imports more expensive for regular Indians.

Increased geopolitical risks and threats to global supply chains typically make FIIs (big foreign investors) nervous, leading them to pull capital out of Indian stocks, which can drag down the market.

watch_next: Further actions or statements by Indonesian energy ministers regarding gas exports
Broader global energy supply disruptions and shipping chokepoint tensions
analysis.caveats: The gas cuts by Indonesia may ultimately have innocent explanations and remain small in scale, meaning regional energy trade could stabilize without major global consequences.

events.article_text:
Severe cyclone Murasu probed Chennai with outer rain bands but skirted the coast on Monday morning as it raced towards the south Andhra Pradesh coast for a landfall beginning midnight tonight. | Photo Credit: www.meteologix.com/in

Severe cycloneMurasu sent its outer rain bands to Chennai while skirting the coast, and is racing towards South Coastal Andhra Pradesh, with landfall expected between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole, around midnight on Monday or in the early hours of Tuesday (by 4 am). Ports along the south Andhra Pradesh coast are on high alert as the storm threatens to unleash damaging winds, storm surges and high waves.

India Meteorological Department (IMD) said Murasu intensified into a severe cyclonic storm and lay over the west-central and adjoining south-west Bay of Bengal at 5.30 am on Monday. Its centre was located about 200 km east-northeast of Chennai; 210 km east-southeast of Nellore; 270 km south-southeast of Machilipatnam; 220 km east-southeast of Kavali; and 260 km southeast of Ongole.

Cyclone Murasu: AP CM Naidu seeks support from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka

Having come closest to the Chennai coast at about 200 km, the cyclone appeared to have skirted the city and was now heading towards its likely landfall zone along the South Andhra coast. The IMD expects it to cross the coast as a severe cyclone, packing sustained wind speeds of 100-110 km/hr and gusts of up to 120 km/hr.

The approaching cyclone has triggered a stepped-up alert across the coastal port infrastructure. Great Danger Signal Number 10, indicating an exceptionally severe threat, has been hoisted at Nizampatnam and Vadarevu ports, while Machilipatnam has been placed under Great Danger Signal Number 9. Krishnapatnam port is under Great Danger Signal Number 8. Visakhapatnam, Bheemunipatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Kalingapatnam ports have hoisted Local Cautionary Signal Number 3.

Bapatla, along with Krishna and Prakasam district on the south Andhra Pradesh coast, is expected to bear the brunt of the storm surge. The IMD has warned that a surge of about 3.2-5 feet above the astronomical tide could inundate low-lying coastal areas of South Andhra Pradesh around the time of landfall.

The threat extends beyond the immediate landfall zone. A high-wave warning has been issued for the East Godavari coast between Antarvedi and Perumallapuram, where waves of 10-16 feet are forecast from 2.30 pm on Monday until 11.30 am on Tuesday. Small vessels have been advised to remain ashore, while nearshore recreational activities must be suspended. Coastal erosion and wave-induced surges are also possible.

Fishing operations have been ordered to remain suspended along the coast. Fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea along or off the coast from Monday through Wednesday. The state Fisheries Department and fishing harbour authorities have been asked to alert fishing communities and closely monitor subsequent IMD marine warnings. Fishermen have also been urged to plan their activities strictly in accordance with the latest area-specific advisories, which will remain crucial as the cyclone approaches and crosses the coast.

the_story: Severe cyclone Murasu skirted Chennai on Monday morning and is heading toward the South Andhra Pradesh coast for a landfall around midnight Monday or 4 am Tuesday between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole.
The IMD (India Meteorological Department, the government weather office) expects the storm to pack sustained winds of 100-110 km/hr with gusts up to 120 km/hr, alongside a storm surge of 3.2-5 feet.
Travel disruptions include 11 cancelled flights in Chennai and 10 in Vijayawada.
Ports have raised severe warnings, including Great Danger Signal Number 10 at Nizampatnam and Vadarevu, and fishing operations are completely suspended along the coast through Wednesday.
analysis.what_happened: A severe cyclonic storm named Murasu formed over the Bay of Bengal and moved northwest. Driven by warm ocean waters and atmospheric conditions, it intensified and traveled toward the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, prompting widespread emergency alerts.
analysis.analogy: It is like a massive roadblock suddenly shutting down the main highway connecting a major farming region to city markets, forcing trucks to halt and causing temporary shortages of everyday goods.
why_it_matters_india: Severe winds and floods disrupt transport and local farming in coastal Andhra Pradesh.
Supply chains for vegetables, fish, and local produce face temporary blockages.
Short-term local supply shortages can push up food prices (inflation, the rate at which general prices rise) in nearby markets.
Infrastructure damage leads to government spending on repairs and relief measures.

impacts.target: Vegetable & food prices in local Andhra markets
impacts.rationale: Storm damage to crops and blocked transport routes make food harder to supply, which is bad for household budgets.

impacts.target: Local transport and logistics stocks (like transport operators)
impacts.rationale: Flight cancellations and port closures halt business activity temporarily, which can hurt near-term earnings.

watch_next: Post-landfall damage reports from the IMD and state government
Updates on port operations and resumption of flights in Chennai and Vijayawada
analysis.caveats: The exact intensity and track of the storm at landfall could change the scale of damage and disruption.

analysis.tldr: The government is spending more than it earns, which could mean it needs to borrow more money, potentially keeping loan interest rates high for regular people.
the_story: India's fiscal deficit (the gap between government spending and earnings) hit Rs 7.14 lakh crore for the first half of the financial year through September.
This deficit has widened to 42.1% of the full-year target set for the financial year.
Total money collected (receipts) reached Rs 18.35 lakh crore, which is 50.3% of the annual estimate.
The government has budgeted a total fiscal deficit of Rs 16.96 lakh crore for the entire year.
Major subsidy expenditures (money paid by the government to keep essential goods cheap) reached approximately Rs 6.55 lakh crore.
analysis.what_happened: The Indian government spent significantly more money than it brought in through taxes and other revenues during the first six months of the financial year. This happened largely because major subsidy expenditures reached about Rs 6.55 lakh crore, widening the budget gap to 42.1% of the full-year target.
analysis.analogy: It's like a household spending heavily on groceries and utility bills early in the year, leaving their credit card bill piling up faster than planned.
why_it_matters_india: A wider budget gap means the government needs extra money to cover its expenses.
To get this money, the government borrows by issuing bonds (formal IOUs or government debt certificates).
When the government borrows heavily, 10-year bond yield (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) tends to rise.
Higher government borrowing costs often keep overall market interest rates high, meaning costlier home and car loans for everyday people.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Higher government borrowing to cover the deficit pushes up yields, which is generally bad for borrowers as it keeps loan rates high.
High government spending on subsidies can circulate more money in the economy, potentially pushing up prices of everyday goods — bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Government tax collection numbers for the second half of the year
Updates on whether the government sticks to its final budget deficit target
analysis.caveats: The article text is very brief and mixes the news with advertisements and unrelated headlines, though the core fiscal figures are clear.

events.headline: The Next Congress Needs to Reclaim Its Oversight of the Department of Defense

items.title: The Next Congress Needs to Reclaim Its Oversight of the Department of Defense
items.summary: Since returning to office in January 2025, the Trump administration has aggressively exercised executive authority across the federal government. Meanwhile, Congress has not adequately applied its oversight role to rein in the executive branch, particularly over the Department of Defense. We have watched these dynamics with specific interest, in discussions with congressional staff over bills and appropriations, and in conversations with our clients.Congress adjourned at the end of September until after the midterm elections following an unproductive summer legislative session, particularly on

events.article_text:
Congress adjourned at the end of September until after the midterm elections following an unproductive summer legislative session, particularly on foreign policy. While Congress passed a long-debated Russia sanctions bill in September, President Donald Trump has already issued a waiver to it in Moscow’s favor. The Senate failed to pass a procedural resolution challenging Trump’s war powers in Iran. Moreover, Congress has done little to advance the defense authorization bill: While the House barely passed its version of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act in July, Senate Democrats blocked their chamber’s version of the bill in protest over the war with Iran in the same month, and have not advanced the bill since. Not coincidentally, Republicans find themselves facing significant election losses, defending their record and a historically unpopular president and administration amidst an ongoing war and executive overreach.

Nowhere has executive expansion been more pronounced than at the Department of Defense, where the administration has asserted broad control over defense contractors, authorized legally dubious strikes on alleged drug smugglers, and conducted decapitation operations against foreign regimes. Recently, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth outlined even more significant expansions of department power and recently declared he will shrink the general/flag officer corps by 20 percent despite bipartisan concerns. Republican leaders have largely acceded to this consolidation of executive power, and their reasons for going along are straightforward. Members of Congress largely live in fear of their voter bases and face the most risk from the president opposing them in primary elections or suppressing the Republican vote in general elections, as demonstrated in the many high-profile primary losses by Republican incumbents this year following Trump endorsements of their opponents.

Yet while the record of the current Congress may seem like continued surrender to the administration’s strategic and fiscal goals for the military, the details of the current dynamic reveal a more complicated situation. Quietly, in the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act and in the evolving FY27 bill, Congress has established tools to reclaim its constitutional role in shaping U.S. defense strategy — relying on procedure, statutory mandates, and funding decisions rather than public confrontation to do so.

While Congress has so far failed to defend the very limits to executive power it authored, the coming months will set the scene for an oversight role amid a more complicated dynamic. With the midterm elections increasingly likely to give Democrats at least partial control of Congress, congressional oversight will be challenging. The administration has announced in response to recent statutes born of the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act that it does not believe Congress has the authority to limit its power or has outright refused to follow congressional direction. Congress cannot legally enforce its statutory requirements over a disobedient executive: It must use its constitutional powers to impose compliance through appropriations, oversight, and even impeachment.

Regardless of how difficult, a future Congress can and should use its powers to limit executive overreach and reassert its role in overseeing national defense.

Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration expanded executive power and concentrated decision-making at a scale with few modern precedents, most prominently within the Department of Defense. Operationally, it executed a series of large-scale military actions — including strikes in Venezuela, expansive maritime interdictions in the Caribbean, and a sustained offensive campaign against Iran — all conducted with little congressional oversight or authorization. At the same time, the administration pursued structural changes to Department of Defense leadership, removing senior civilian and uniformed leaders at an unprecedented pace while advancing plans to remove additional military leaders and merge U.S. Northern Command and Southern Command into a new Western Hemisphere Command. Major acquisition programs and contracts were also canceled or restructured, while defense contractors have been subjected to heightened Department of Defense control, which may be inconsistent with existing statutory and regulatory frameworks.

These shifts — and the tensions between the executive and legislative branches — were first and most clearly reflected in the documents that now define U.S. defense strategy: the 2025 National Security Strategy, the 2026 National Defense Strategy, and the recent National Defense Authorization Acts.

The 2025 National Security Strategy marked a decisive narrowing of U.S. global influence. Adding narrative structure to President Trump’s own strategic instincts, it rejected post-Cold War assumptions of global primacy in favor of regional balances of power and selective engagement in world affairs. In a break from what has historically been U.S. defense strategy to focus on threats posed by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, the National Security Strategy prioritized the Western Hemisphere, homeland defense, migration control, and economic security. China was framed as a competitor to be managed rather than a systemic adversary threatening democratic nations, and allies were similarly viewed as transactional partners: pay more for defense or face less U.S. commitment. Ironically, the administration’s war against Iran highlights its lack of consistency within any strategic framework.

The 2026 National Defense Strategy, directed by longtime China hawk Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, attempted to reconcile this worldview with operational realities. history.title: A state-encouraged bubble and a surprise devaluation
history.what: Chinese shares doubled in a year, partly on state media encouragement, then fell about 40% in three months. In August the central bank unexpectedly devalued the yuan, and world markets fell sharply over two days.
history.why: Retail investors, many with newly opened accounts and little experience, had bought heavily on margin loans. When prices turned, margin calls forced selling, which forced more margin calls. The devaluation then signalled that China's slowdown was worse than official figures admitted, which hit everyone selling into Chinese demand.
history.impact: Commodities collapsed — copper, iron ore and oil all fell hard, since China consumed roughly half the world's industrial metals. Emerging market currencies including the rupee weakened. Indian metal shares fell sharply despite nothing changing in India.
history.policy: Trading halts, a ban on large shareholders selling, state funds instructed to buy, and tighter capital controls to stop money leaving. Later, a managed and better-communicated currency mechanism.
history.consequence: It exposed the limits of administrative intervention in a market: the measures slowed the fall but damaged foreign investors' trust in Chinese market access for years. That trust deficit is part of why global money has been reallocating toward India since.
history.pattern: Retail leverage is the accelerant. A market where ordinary investors are buying with borrowed money does not correct gently, because the selling is involuntary. Margin data is one of the few genuinely predictive warnings.
history.india_echo: Worth watching Indian margin funding and futures-and-options participation, both of which have grown enormously since 2020. For that risk, 2015 China is the more relevant precedent than 2008 America.
history.watch_for: Rapid growth in new trading accounts alongside rising borrowed positions. That pair has preceded every retail-driven unwind.
